evidence: Draft judged: "Conscious agreement, unconscious receptivity, emotional compliance, legal and ethical consent - can people have their minds influenced without the conscious agreement of their adult self?" Compared word for word with the words it replaces ("...legal and ethical consent. Can people have their minds influenced without conscious agreement of their adult self?"): the only differences are ". Can" becoming " - can" (the dash join the_change names) and a "the" before "conscious agreement" (a function word the_change does not name, within what it calls Emulate's version; it does not change the sense). The four kinds, the question, "their minds" and "adult self" are all intact, nothing is dropped, and nothing is added: no claim, name, number or first-person fact. So SOURCE's meaning (a mind can be influenced without the adult self having clearly chosen it; four kinds of agreement) is kept exactly as far as the replaced words kept it. The draft occurs once in CONTEXT.txt (line 7) and is verbatim there. In context it follows the paragraph above, which has just said people can be influenced "without engaging their conscious mind" and describes, through the FTC and the OECD, designs that "manipulate people toward choices that may work against their interests"; a question about conscious agreement and "legal and ethical consent" is therefore prepared, not abrupt, and the Silva Mind Control quote after it ("someone else will!") continues the same worry. On the dash: it is a plain spaced hyphen, not an em dash, and a list joined to its question this way reads as ordinary casual punctuation. The paragraph above has the same spaced hyphen in its FTC sentence, but per the_change for G-S14 that sentence is part of Emulate's proposed text, so I do not lean on it as the article's own habit. Pronouns: "their" is people, "their adult self" is each person's own; no stray referent. A first-time reader can read it in one pass, as a list-then-question in a casual blog register. Tell rows: I find none actually PRESENT. Looked at hardest: T12 and T21 (a four-term list inside one 26-word sentence): the four terms are his published four and are what the question turns on, not a taxonomy made for balance, and the sentence has one job (the question) with the list as its topic, so the operation is not happening; T26 ("conscious agreement" twice in one sentence, "conscious" also in the paragraph above): the second use is the question pointing back at the first item and the conscious/unconscious contrast is the topic, so the repeat does a job; T24 and T25 (dash plus question): the question is not answered at once and the dash follows a real list, not a bare noun phrase; T03: the paragraph above sets up the consent question; T02, T09, T13: one line with one list and one question, no run of compressed teaching beats, and it draws a distinction (conscious agreement against the other three) rather than filling a slot; T14 and T15: no reordering and no word swaps, only punctuation and a determiner; T04, T05, T08: no scene, prop or image; T01, T06, T07, T10, T11, T16-T20, T22, T23, T27-T29 not present (no first person, filler, negative reveal, announcing line, closing line or tic word). C01-C04 absent: no "kid", no stray referent, no first-person fact, no named-entity claim in the draft itself. Linter: "B4/E15 list or packed sentence" accepted, because the list is the source's own list kept verbatim, the replaced words already had it as a fragment, and joining it to the question adds no second argumentative job. "D9 follows the source order" accepted, because this is a one-sentence replacement of one sentence, so following its order is by construction; T13 and T09 checked as above. One note on the writer's ledger: its T14 evidence says the change "puts back the author's own point that Emulate dropped" and its T15 evidence says it "puts back the author's words or meaning"; neither describes this change (Emulate's version with a dash join, no put-back). That does not affect the verdict.
